pattern: Self-feeding work pipeline with external politeness: a prioritised frontier feeds per-target queues that enforce rate limits on systems you don't own, stateless workers do the I/O, outputs land in cheap bulk storage, and compact probabilistic sets stop the loop from redoing work.

tips.nudge: What does this system do, start to finish, for one URL?
tips.hint: Describe the loop: take a URL, get the page, find new URLs.
tips.show: F1: Starting from seed URLs, fetch HTML pages, store them, extract links and add new URLs to crawl.

checks.label: Obligations toward the sites being visited

tips.nudge: Site owners complained about something specific.
tips.hint: Capture the per-host rate and the rules sites publish.
tips.show: N1: Polite: ≤ 1 request/s per host and obey robots.txt (allow/disallow, crawl-delay).

tips.nudge: A third of pages are copies, and links point to the same URL millions of times.
tips.hint: Say what must not be fetched or stored twice.
tips.show: F2: Each URL is fetched once per crawl cycle; pages with duplicate content are detected and not stored/indexed twice.

tips.nudge: 2B pages a month is how many per second?
tips.hint: pages per month ÷ seconds per month, then a peak factor.
tips.show: 2B / 2.6M s ≈ 770 pages/s; plan for ~1,500/s peak.

tips.nudge: Pages per month × size × months kept.
tips.hint: Decide whether duplicates are stored; compression helps but estimate raw first.
tips.show: 2B × 100 KB × 6 months ≈ 1.2 PB (≈ 800 TB after dropping duplicates; less compressed).

tips.nudge: Pages per second × bytes per page.
tips.hint: Convert to bits per second.
tips.show: 770 pages/s × 100 KB ≈ 77 MB/s ≈ 0.6 Gbps average, ~1.2 Gbps peak.

tips.nudge: The crawler is internal. Who tells it where to start, or to recrawl a site now?
tips.hint: Define a small control API for seeds and per-host policies.
tips.show: POST /seeds {urls[], priority} → 202; PUT /hosts/{host}/policy {max_rps, enabled}

tips.nudge: What does the crawler know about every URL it hasn't fetched yet, or must refetch?
tips.hint: Model the URL record that decides when it's fetched next.
tips.show: url_meta(url_hash PK, url, host, priority, last_fetched, next_fetch_at, content_hash, status) + the frontier queues.

tips.nudge: What exactly does the indexing team read?
tips.hint: Raw content plus enough metadata to find and reprocess it.
tips.show: pages: blob key = url_hash/fetch_time → compressed HTML + headers; batched into large files (WARC-style).

checks.label: What gets fetched next, and when, designed as its own part

tips.nudge: A single FIFO of URLs is full of links to the same big site. What happens to that site?
tips.hint: Add a part for the frontier: compare a global FIFO, per-fetcher sleeps, and queues grouped by host with a release time.
tips.show: Part 'URL frontier': priority front queues → per-host back queues; a heap of 'host ready at t' hands each host to one fetcher at ≤1 req/s (or robots crawl-delay); robots.txt cached per host.

checks.label: Downloading at scale designed as its own part

tips.nudge: ~1,500 fetches per second, each taking about a second. How many are in flight, and what happens before each one?
tips.hint: Add a part for the fetchers: compare thread-per-fetch with async I/O, and say how hostnames are resolved.
tips.show: Part 'Fetchers and DNS': async HTTP fetchers leasing URLs from the frontier, a local caching DNS resolver, strict timeouts.

checks.label: Detecting repeats designed as its own part

tips.nudge: An exact hash set of 20B URLs needs how much memory? And what about copies with one changed byte?
tips.hint: Add a part that separates URL-level dedup from content-level dedup.
tips.show: Part 'Dedup': normalise URLs (strip tracking params, lowercase host) then check a Bloom filter; content: exact hash for copies, SimHash for near-duplicates.

checks.label: Freshness designed as its own part

tips.nudge: News changes hourly, most pages rarely. Should every page be refetched on the same schedule?
tips.hint: Add a part for recrawling: what sets a URL's revisit interval and what re-enqueues it.
tips.show: Part 'Recrawl scheduling': priority = importance × staleness; revisit interval adapts to observed change rate (halve when changed, double when not); a scheduler re-enqueues due URLs from url_meta.

checks.label: Something orders and paces the work

tips.nudge: Thousands of fetchers need to know what to fetch next. Who tells them?
tips.hint: A durable structure of URLs waiting, with a policy on what comes out next.
tips.show: URL frontier: priority queues in front, per-host queues behind, a scheduler releasing each host at most 1/s.

checks.label: Storage for petabytes of raw content

tips.nudge: 1.2 PB of write-once, read-in-bulk data. Which kind of store?
tips.hint: Cheap, durable, large objects; append and batch reads.
tips.show: Object/blob storage (S3/HDFS-like), pages batched into large files.

checks.label: Per-fetch overheads besides the download kept cheap

tips.nudge: Before every fetch you must turn a hostname into an IP. How slow can that be?
tips.hint: Standard resolvers are slow and synchronous at this rate.
tips.show: A local caching DNS resolver per fetcher cluster (TTL-respecting), resolving asynchronously.

checks.label: Fast membership test for what's been seen

tips.nudge: Every extracted link: 'have we got this URL already?' out of 20 billion.
tips.hint: A compact set in memory that can say 'definitely new' quickly.
tips.show: Seen-URL Bloom filter (~25 GB for 20B URLs at 1% false positives) + content fingerprint store.

tips.nudge: Where do pages actually come from in your diagram?
tips.hint: Draw the internet as an external node and connect the component that downloads.
tips.show: Fetcher workers → websites (HTTP GET with timeouts).

checks.label: Discovered links feed back into the work

tips.nudge: The crawler finds most of its URLs itself. How do they get back in?
tips.hint: Close the loop from link extraction to the frontier.
tips.show: Parser → seen filter → frontier priority queues (only new URLs).

tips.nudge: A site has a calendar with a 'next month' link on every page. How long does your crawler stay there?
tips.hint: Decide which limits or signals stop the crawler from following a generated, infinite URL space.
tips.show: Max depth, max URL length and a page budget per host per cycle; demote hosts whose new pages are mostly near-duplicates.

tips.nudge: Which component saturates first as you add fetchers?
tips.hint: Look at DNS, the frontier, the seen-filter and politeness itself.
tips.show: DNS (cache), the frontier (shard by host hash), the Bloom filter (partition by URL hash), and politeness: big sites cap throughput, so crawl many hosts in parallel.

tips.nudge: A fetcher crashes holding 200 URLs. A site returns 503 for an hour. A trap generates infinite URLs.
tips.hint: Cover worker loss, unhealthy hosts, traps and frontier durability.
tips.show: Leases on dequeued URLs (redelivered if not acked); per-host backoff on 5xx/timeouts; max depth/URL length/pages per host against traps; frontier persisted to disk with checkpoints.
